Your agent can learn a database it has never seen, prepare a schema change
against it, and follow that change to completion. The pieces it needs are
already here: a schema it can read, a plan it can check before anything runs,
and structured output it can parse.

This page has two halves. The first is what to give your agent so it can do
that work well. The second is where the decision stays with you.

## Install the agent skill

[`skills/schemabot`](../skills/schemabot/SKILL.md) is a ready-made agent skill
and the fastest way to get a useful agent. It covers how to edit schema files,
read a plan, drive a pull request through its environments, and unblock a check
that is waiting on something.

Its [command policy](../skills/schemabot/references/command-policy.md) spells
out, for every PR comment command, whether your agent posts it, asks you first,
or hands it to you. That policy is the complete list; the rest of this page
explains the reasoning behind it.

The skill is a standard `SKILL.md` directory in the
[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format, which agents such as Claude
Code, Codex, and goose load. Copy the directory into the place your agent loads
skills from: for Claude Code, that is `.claude/skills/` in your repository or
`~/.claude/skills/`; other agents document their own location. Copy it from a
release tag rather than `main`, so the skill matches the SchemaBot version you
run and a change on `main` reaches your agent only when you upgrade.

Every `schemabot` command the skill writes out, in a code block or as inline
code, is checked in CI against the PR comment parser and the CLI, so an example
that SchemaBot would not accept fails the build.

## What your agent can do

### Learn a database

Your agent does not need to be told what your schema looks like. It can ask.

| Question | Where it looks |
|---|---|
| What databases are there, on which engines and environments? | `databases` |
| What is in this one right now? | `pull`, which returns the live schema as SQL or JSON. `onboard` writes it into a new declarative schema directory |
| What is running at this moment? | `status`, which lists every active apply above the most recent finished ones, and `locks` for what is held |
| What has run against it, and what did one of those do? | `status -d <database>` for the apply history, then `status <apply_id>` and `logs <apply_id>` |
| What DDL has been proposed for it? | `list-plans`, which returns stored plans whether or not they were applied |

[Schema intelligence](schema-intelligence.md) walks through each of these,
including structured columns and indexes, lint findings on the live schema,
and databases that span several targets. The same answers are available over
HTTP, so an agent with no shell can use them.

### Prepare a change

Your agent edits the declarative `CREATE TABLE` files to the end state you
want. It never writes an `ALTER` statement or a numbered change script, which
removes the step agents are worst at.

`plan` then returns the exact DDL SchemaBot would run, along with the lint
findings for it, before anything touches the database. That is the review
surface: your agent can read what it is about to cause, and so can you.
Creating a plan takes write access, so a read-only agent reads the DDL from
the comment SchemaBot posts on the pull request, where it plans on its own, or
from a stored plan it finds with `list-plans`.

### Follow a change

Once a change is running, `progress --no-watch` reports how far along it is,
`logs` returns the lifecycle log for that apply, and `status` gives the current
state. Bare `progress` opens the interactive watcher instead, and its keys stop
or cancel the apply, run its cutover, and close its revert window — an operator
surface, not a read, so an agent following a change passes `--no-watch`.
For a change that spans several targets or shards, each one reports separately,
so an agent can tell you which shard is behind rather than only that something
is. `logs --target` and `--shard` narrow the log to one of them; see
[Read the logs](cli.md#read-the-logs).

### Read all of it as data

These commands emit JSON, so your agent does not have to parse a table meant
for a terminal.

| Commands | JSON option |
|---|---|
| `databases`, `status`, `list-plans`, `logs`, `plan`, `init`, `checks show` | `--json` |
| `pull` | `-o json` |

`apply -o json` streams progress rather than returning one document, and
`progress` has no JSON option of its own — use `status --json` for a structured
snapshot. [Using the CLI from scripts and agents](cli.md#use-the-cli-from-scripts-and-agents)
has the rest of the output options, and the
[schema intelligence guide](schema-intelligence.md) is the read-only API
reference for the same answers over HTTP.

## Give it its own account

How your agent authenticates decides what the record of its work means.

- **With its own account**, give it read-only access to inspect schemas and
  follow changes. The [authentication guide](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service)
  explains how to set this up. This is the better arrangement: its reads are
  attributable, and it cannot write even by mistake.
- **With your account**, its actions are recorded as yours. If it runs the CLI
  with your credentials or posts a comment from your GitHub account, SchemaBot
  cannot tell whether you or your agent sent the command.

The guidance below is a cautious starting point you can adapt for your team.
It includes instructions you can give your agent and settings you can enforce
on the server.

## You decide what runs in production

Let your agent prepare the change and explain what will happen. Under the
policy below, you run the production command yourself. That keeps the final
decision with you and makes the recorded action match who took it.

PR approval is a separate check. Where the review gate is enabled, SchemaBot
requires approval before applying a change. That check still applies
when an agent sends the command, but it cannot tell whether you reviewed what
your agent is about to do with your credentials.

## Decide when your agent should ask

| Task | Suggested boundary |
|---|---|
| Run a production command such as `apply`, `apply-confirm`, `cutover`, or `rollback` | You run it yourself, even if you previously asked the agent to do it |
| Run a command with `--allow-unsafe`, in any environment | You review the destructive change and run the command yourself |
| Ask to override a freeze with `--override`, in any environment | You decide whether to ask, write the reason, and run the command yourself. See [guidance for agents](freeze.md#guidance-for-agents) |
| Apply to a shared staging database or one that other teams depend on | Your agent hands you the command |
| Apply to a new or isolated staging database with little impact on others | Your agent explains what it will do, then proceeds |
| Apply when it is unclear who depends on the database | Your agent hands you the command |
| Inspect status, progress, history, a stored plan, or the live schema | Your agent can use its read access without asking each time |

If you prefer to run every write command yourself, say so in your agent's
instructions. That takes precedence over the staging defaults above.

Staging changes can affect other people too. A change can disrupt their tests
or hold a database lock while it runs. Use your team's service criticality
ratings if you have them; otherwise, treat any staging database you cannot
confirm is isolated as shared. Any configured approval requirements still apply.

## Give your agent clear instructions

You can copy this into your agent's instructions:

> - Prepare production commands for me to review and run. Do not execute them,
>   even if I ask you to.
> - Do not run commands with `--allow-unsafe`. Show me the change and the exact
>   command so I can decide and run it myself.
> - Do not ask to override a freeze with `--override`. Tell me what is frozen
>   and give me the command.
> - Before applying to staging, check who depends on the database. If it is
>   shared, critical, or unclear, give me the command instead of running it. For
>   a new or isolated database with little impact on others, explain what you
>   will do before proceeding.
> - If I say I will run all write commands myself, follow that preference.
> - Use your read access to inspect status, progress, stored plans, history,
>   and live schemas. Follow a change with `status` or `progress --no-watch`,
>   because the interactive watcher's keys change the apply. Creating a new
>   plan requires write access.
> - If a request returns `403`, explain the missing permission. Do not try other
>   credentials or disable authentication to get around it. Ask an operator to
>   check whether the account should have access.
> - Propose schema changes by editing the schema files in a pull request, where
>   I can review the plan and follow the checks.

## Back it up with server settings

Instructions guide your agent. Server settings control what it can do with
the credentials you give it. They cannot make an action “human only” when
the agent uses your credentials.

- **Give services their own read-only access.** With a service mesh, `forward_auth`
  can limit requests from listed services to reads. With OIDC, keep admin groups out
  of service tokens: a token with an admin group can write, even when it
  belongs to a service. See [service access](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service).
- **Choose which accounts can run PR commands.** Enable
  `pr_command_authorization` and leave bot accounts out of admin and operator
  grants when you want them to remain read-only. Check repository-level admin
  grants too. See [GitHub permissions](auth.md#github-side-authorization).
- **Require review before apply.** Enable
  [`review_policy`](configuration.md#review-gate) to require a qualifying
  approval for the environments served by that instance, or a database's
  own `review_policy` to require one for that database alone. The PR
  author's own approval does not count. An approval keeps counting after
  later pushes until the reviewer requests changes or GitHub dismisses it. Set `require_reapproval: true` to
  require a new approval when the PR's schema change differs from the one
  approved.
- **Review destructive changes before allowing them.** Changes flagged as unsafe
  require `--allow-unsafe` to proceed. If your agent uses your credentials, it
  can supply that flag too—SchemaBot cannot tell whether you personally
  approved the change.
- **Check the logs when a command is denied.** They explain why it was blocked
  and help you check the caller's permissions. The
  `schemabot.pr_command_actor_authorization.total` metric can help you spot
  patterns across requests.
